summary: Defines Digest Access Authentication for HTTP, an alternative to Basic authentication, which sends passwords in clear text. Digest uses a challenge and a hash so the password itself is not sent. It was replaced by RFC 2617.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of saying your password aloud, you show a scrambled answer that proves you know it.

questions: how is digest different from basic auth
how does digest prevent password theft
what is a nonce in digest auth
subtitle: Authentication without sending passwords in the clear.

tldr.problem: HTTP Basic authentication sends passwords as clear text, which is insecure if an attacker can sniff the network. A better method is needed that prevents eavesdroppers from learning passwords.
tldr.mechanism: Digest authentication uses a challenge-response scheme: the server sends a nonce value, the client computes an MD5 hash of the username, password, nonce, HTTP method and URI, and sends only the hash (not the password). The server verifies it by computing the same hash.
tldr.outcome: Passwords are never sent over the network, making network snooping attacks much less effective. It was superseded by RFC 2617, which refined the mechanism.

today: RFC 2069 was obsoleted by RFC 2617, which is now the standard for HTTP Digest authentication. Digest auth remains in use for WebDAV and some SIP applications, though session-based authentication and OAuth are more common on the modern web.

sections.title: The Problem with Basic Authentication
sections.content:
HTTP's Basic authentication sends the username and password with every request, encoded only as base64. An attacker who captures network traffic can decode this and obtain the user's password immediately. If that user reuses the password elsewhere, the attacker gains access to all their accounts.

RFC 2069 defines Digest authentication as a replacement. Instead of transmitting the password, the client sends a checksum (digest) that proves it knows the password, without revealing it to eavesdroppers.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic auth is like writing your password on a postcard; anyone who sees it can read it. Digest auth is like writing a secret code that only proves you know the password, but does not reveal it.

sections.title: How Digest Authentication Works
sections.content:
Digest authentication uses a challenge-response mechanism. When a client first requests a protected resource, the server responds with a 401 Unauthorized status and sends a challenge in the WWW-Authenticate header. The challenge includes a realm (which resource is being protected), a unique nonce value (number used once), and optionally other fields like the hashing algorithm.

The client computes a response digest by hashing the username, password, realm, nonce, HTTP method, and the requested URI together using MD5. It sends this hash back in the Authorization header, along with the username and nonce. The server repeats the same computation using the password from its database and verifies that the computed hash matches the one sent by the client.

Crucially, an eavesdropper who sees the hash cannot deduce the password, and cannot reuse the hash for a different URI or HTTP method, because the hash includes those values.
sections.plainLanguage: The server gives a puzzle (the nonce), and the client mixes it with their password and hashes it together. The client sends the hashed answer, but not the password. The server checks the answer matches what it computed with the correct password.

sections.title: Headers and Message Formats
sections.content:
Digest authentication uses three HTTP headers:

WWW-Authenticate (server challenge): The server sends this when the client is not authenticated. It includes the realm, a nonce value, and optionally an opaque field (data the client must return unchanged) and a stale flag (indicating whether the nonce has expired).

Authorization (client response): The client sends this with the username, realm, nonce, the requested URI, and the computed response digest. An optional digest field can be included to verify the integrity of the response body.

Authentication-Info (optional server response): After successful authentication, the server may send this to provide a new nonce for the next request or a digest of the response body for integrity checking.

The response digest is computed as a hash of the nonce and a derived value called A1 (the hash of username:realm:password). This approach lets servers store only A1 instead of plain passwords, so even if the password file is compromised, an attacker must still perform a brute-force attack to recover passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a puzzle (nonce) in the challenge. The client sends back the answer (digest) plus their username. The server can also tell the client a new puzzle for the next request.

sections.title: Security Compared to Basic Authentication
sections.content:
Digest authentication is far superior to Basic authentication. An eavesdropper listening to the network can no longer obtain the user's password directly. However, digest authentication remains a weak scheme by modern cryptographic standards.

The nonce prevents simple replay attacks. If the server constructs the nonce to include the client's IP address, a timestamp, and a secret key, then replaying a captured digest from a different IP address or after the timestamp expires will fail. More aggressive approaches can use one-time nonces or one-time digests to prevent replay attacks entirely, but at the cost of server overhead.

The scheme is still vulnerable to some attacks. A man-in-the-middle attacker could replace the digest challenge with a Basic challenge to trick the client into sending a password. Digest authentication does not encrypt the request body, only authenticate the client. For sensitive data, SSL/TLS encryption is required.

Password storage matters: the server must protect the password file as carefully as if it contained plain-text passwords, because a compromised password file immediately grants access to resources in its realm.
sections.plainLanguage: Digest is much safer than Basic, because eavesdroppers cannot steal your password. But it is still not perfect: you need to trust the network path to the server, and SSL should be used for truly sensitive data.

sections.title: Status and Obsolescence
sections.content:
RFC 2069 was obsoleted by RFC 2617, published in 1999, which refined the mechanism and added more features. The newer RFC is now the standard definition of HTTP Digest authentication.

Digest authentication is less common than it once was. Modern web applications typically use session cookies (protected by TLS) or OAuth for authentication, which are simpler for users and often more flexible for application developers. However, digest authentication is still used in some contexts, such as WebDAV and SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Digest auth was improved in a newer RFC, and most web sites now use different methods like login cookies. But some applications still use digest auth because it works well for them.
